intro: Foundations of International Law. Unit eleven: self-determination and human rights.

slides.4: External and internal self-determination. External self-determination is the right to establish one's own state, and it is the contested half. Secession is accepted in the colonial context; outside it, the most that is argued is remedial secession as an ultima ratio, in cases of serious, systematic and widespread human rights violations — a claim the International Court of Justice pointedly did not resolve in the Kosovo advisory opinion. Internal self-determination is the safer half: free choice of one's own status and of the political, economic, social and cultural order, without outside interference — which is why it is tied to the prohibition of intervention. Whether it extends to a right of political participation, or to autonomy for ethnic minorities, is open.
slides.6: Human rights versus diplomatic protection — the clearest way to see what human rights changed. Diplomatic protection is a right of the state to have its own nationals protected abroad, the law on the treatment of foreigners, and nationality is decisive. Human rights are rights of the individual against their own state; nationality is irrelevant and the individual is the holder. Two consequences follow: the individual is no longer mediatized by their own state, and they can enforce the rights themselves — through quasi-judicial procedures in the United Nations system and individual complaints before regional courts. One more pairing worth holding: human rights apply in peacetime and in armed conflict; humanitarian law applies only in conflict.
